main/charsequence.html.title: CharSequence
main/charsequence.html.description:
Are Character-Based Objects Interface implemented by String, StringBuilder, and StringBuffer Provides a common way to work with sequences of characters Fun fact: Methods belonging to CharSequence
These methods are implemented/overridden by its implementing classes
String is Immutable Once created, its value cannot be changed Any modification creates a new String object Good for values that don't need frequent modification String literals can be stored in the String Pool StringBuilder is mutable Uses capacity — extra memory reserved for future characters More efficient than String when repeatedly modifying text Not thread-safe Generally preferred for single-threaded string manipulation StringBuffer is mutable Similar functionality to StringBuilder Methods are synchronized, making it thread-safe Generally slower than StringBuilder because of synchronization Useful when multiple threads may modify the same character sequence length() → returns the number of characters charAt(index) → returns the character at a given index subSequence(start, end) → returns part of the character sequence toString() → converts the sequence into a String equals() → compares string contents equalsIgnoreCase() → compares contents ignoring case compareTo() → lexicographically compares strings contains() → checks if a sequence exists startsWith() / endsWith() → checks the beginning/end of a string indexOf() → finds the position of a character/substring substring() → extracts part of a string replace() → replaces characters or sequences split() → divides a string into an array trim() → removes leading/trailing whitespace toUpperCase() / toLowerCase() → changes letter case append() → adds characters to the end insert() → inserts characters at a position delete() → removes characters deleteCharAt() → removes one character replace() → replaces part of the sequence reverse() → reverses the sequence setCharAt() → changes a character setLength() → changes the length capacity() → returns the current capacity String → don't need to modify StringBuilder → need to modify, single thread StringBuffer → *need to modify, multiple threads

main/containers.html.title: Containers
main/containers.html.description: Prone to memory leaks Resources may not be properly released if containers are not managed correctly. Volatile (impermanent) Data stored in containers may be temporary and can disappear when the container or program is terminated. Collections of elements with no duplicates. Elements are unique. Common operations: Union — combines elements from two sets. Intersection — returns elements common to both sets. Difference — returns elements that exist in one set but not another. A linear data structure that follows LIFO (Last In, First Out). You can: Push — add an item to the top. Pop — remove the top item. Peek/Top — view the top item without removing it. Only the top item is directly accessible. Can be implemented using an array or linked list. A hierarchical data structure consisting of nodes connected by edges. Similar to a real tree: Root → trunk/base Branches → connections Leaves → nodes with no children Examples: File systems Organization charts Search trees Note: A tree is not the same as a hashmap. An associative array abstract data type that maps keys to values. Example: studentID → studentName username → password Uses a hash function to convert a key into an index. The index points to a bucket or slot in an underlying array. Allows fast insertion, lookup, and deletion on average. Hash collisions occur when different keys produce the same index; collision-handling methods include chaining and open addressing.s

main/de-morgan's-law.html.description:
describe how logical NOT (¬) interacts with AND (∧) and OR (∨). They are useful when simplifying or transforming logical expressions.
NOT (A OR B) = NOT A AND NOT B
NOT (A AND B) = NOT A OR NOT B
In programming notation:!(A || B) = !A && !B !(A && B) = !A || !B
When a NOT is distributed across a logical expression:
AND becomes OR
OR becomes AND
Each operand is negated

main/formatting.html.title: Formatting
main/formatting.html.description:
Use 4 spaces as the unit of indentation. Tabs are discouraged unless the project's conventions specify otherwise. If tabs are used, configure them to represent 8 spaces. Avoid lines longer than 80 characters. When breaking a long line: Break after a comma when possible. Break before an operator when appropriate. Align continuation lines with the beginning of the expression. If alignment becomes confusing, use an additional 8-space indentation. Use blank lines to separate logical sections. Separate classes with 2 blank lines.
Do not insert a blank line between a Class declaration and its first method.
Separate methods with 1 blank line.
Separate local variable declarations from the first statement with 1 blank line. Use a blank line before a block or single-line comment when appropriate.
Separate logical sections within a method with 1 blank line. A statement is roughly equivalent to a sentence in natural language. Statements are generally terminated with a semicolon (;).
Statements must occur within an appropriate code block, such as a method body. Example:int age = 20; System.out.println(age);

main/grammar-and-syntax.html.title: Grammar and Syntax
main/grammar-and-syntax.html.description:
Syntax refers to the rules that determine how symbols/tokens can be arranged to form valid programs or statements.
Uses: Alphabet — the set of allowed symbols.
Lexicon — the collection of valid words/tokens.
Sequences of symbols or tokens — arranged according to syntactic rules. Defines the rules for creating acceptable grammar/structures in a language.
A Context-Free Grammar (CFG) is a formal system used to describe the syntax of programming languages.
Syntax trees (parse trees) represent the hierarchical structure of a program or expression. They show how operations and components are organized according to the grammar.
The hierarchy of operations can be represented visually through the tree. Grammar is a set of rules that defines how valid statements or expressions can be formed in a language.
In programming languages, grammar determines whether a sequence of tokens is syntactically valid.
CFG is commonly used to formally describe programming-language grammar. Interpretation The program is executed statement by statement, sequentially, by an interpreter.
The interpreter translates/executes instructions as the program runs. Compilation The program is translated before execution into another form, such as machine code or intermediate code.
The resulting code can then be executed. Linker Combines separately compiled pieces of machine/object code into a single executable program.
It can also resolve references between separately compiled modules or libraries before execution. Java Translation Java uses compiler to translate source into bytecode
Then uses Java Virtual Machine (JVM) to interpret bytecode (execution) Since bytecode is low-level and easy to interpret, JVM is small Translation flow:
Source Code → Compiler → Bytecode → JVM → Hardware Source code — program written by the programmer.
Compiler — translates source code into intermediate code.
Intermediate code — platform-independent representation.
Virtual machine — executes the intermediate code.
Simulator/Hardware — ultimately carries out the operations.

main/java-methods-and-functions.html.title: Java Methods and Functions
main/java-methods-and-functions.html.description:
Similar syntax to C, except for modifiers. Method names must use Camel Case. Method names should always be verbs. A method can perform an action, calculate a value, or return information. A function is a method that has a return type. If a method has a return type other than void, it must have a return statement. Syntax: <modifier> <type> methodName(<parameterList>) { return <value>; } public int addNumbers(int a, int b) { return a + b; } public → modifier int → return type addNumbers → method name int a, int b → parameter list return a + b; → returns the result A method with the return type void does not return a value. It can perform an action without giving a result back. public void displayMessage() { System.out.println("Hello!"); } The main method is the entry point of a Java program. It is where the program begins execution. Standard syntax: public static void main(String[] args) { // statements } public → accessible from outside the Class static → can be called without creating an object void → does not return a value main → special method name recognized by Java String[] args → stores command-line arguments Note: The main method is not a special kind of thread. It is a special method that serves as the program's starting point. The JVM invokes it to begin execution.

main/modules-and-lambda-calculus.html.title: Modules and Lambda Calculus
main/modules-and-lambda-calculus.html.description:
Modules help organize a program by dividing code into smaller, reusable structures. Two common types are procedures and functions.A procedure is a named block of code that performs a specific task. Organizes monolithic code into smaller, manageable structures. Improves readability, maintainability, and code reuse. Generally does not return a value directly. May accept parameters and may modify values through output/reference parameters. Does not fundamentally change the overall process flow; it encapsulates a set of operations. CALL procedureName(arguments) A function is a reusable block of code that accepts input and returns a value. Derived from the mathematical concept of a function: input → output. Accepts input through parameters. Performs a computation or operation. Returns a value to the caller. Can be used as part of an expression. SET variableName = functionName(arguments) A lambda function is an anonymous function—a function defined without explicitly giving it a name. It is useful for creating small functions on the fly, especially when a function is needed only temporarily or as an argument to another function.lambda x: x * 2 This represents a function that: accepts x as its parameter returns x * 2 Anonymous — normally does not have an explicit function name. Single-expression — typically contains one expression whose value is returned. First-class — can be assigned to Variables, passed as arguments, and returned from other functions. Lightweight — convenient for short, simple operations. FUNCTION square(x) RETURN x * x END FUNCTION Equivalent lambda-style expression:lambda x: x * x A lambda is best suited for short, simple operations. For complex logic, a regular named function is generally clearer.seealso
Scoping
Parameters and Arguments

main/native-method-process.html.title: Native Method Process
main/native-method-process.html.description:
The general idea is that native methods communicate with C/C++ code used to run embedded systems or the like. In Eclipse: Create a Java Project
Create a Calculator class Declare the native methods using native:
public native int add(int a, int b); Load the native library:
static { System.loadLibrary("calculator");
} Compile the Java class with:
javac -h . Calculator.java This generates:
Calculator.h The .h file contains the JNI function declarations that C/C++ needs to implement. In Eclipse: File → New → C/C++ Project
Create a C/C++ project for the native code. Example structure:
CalculatorNative/
├── src/
│ └── Calculator.c
├── include/
│ └── Calculator.h
└── CMakeLists.txt Copy the generated Calculator.h into the include folder. C/C++ needs the JNI headers from the JDK.
Located at:
<JAVA_HOME>/include
<JAVA_HOME>/include/win32 Important files: jni.h
jni_md.h In Eclipse: Project → Properties
C/C++ General → Paths and Symbols
Add: <JAVA_HOME>/include
<JAVA_HOME>/include/win32
Your project's include folder In Calculator.c:
#include "Calculator.h" JNIEXPORT jint JNICALL Java_Calculator_add( JNIEnv *env, jobject obj, jint a, jint b
) { return a + b;
} The function name comes from the generated Calculator.h. CMake will compile the C/C++ code into a DLL.
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.15) project(Calculator C) add_library(calculator SHARED src/Calculator.c
) target_include_directories(calculator PRIVATE include "$ENV{JAVA_HOME}/include" "$ENV{JAVA_HOME}/include/win32"
) SHARED tells CMake to create a shared library.
On Windows, this produces:
calculator.dll Open a terminal in the C/C++ project directory.
Run:
cmake -S . -B build
cmake --build build The DLL will be created inside the build directory. Java needs to know where calculator.dll is located.
In Eclipse: Run → Run Configurations
Select your Java Application
Go to Arguments
Under VM arguments, add: -Djava.library.path=C:\path\to\CalculatorNative\build Java can now find the DLL when this runs:
System.loadLibrary("calculator"); Run the Java application from Eclipse.
Java calls:
Calculator.add() JNI connects it to:
Java_Calculator_add() The C function executes and returns the result to Java. Java JVM and DLL must have the same architecture: 64-bit Java → 64-bit DLL
32-bit Java → 32-bit DLL System.loadLibrary("calculator") does not include .dll.
For C++, JNI functions should use extern "C" to prevent C++ name mangling.

main/parameters-and-arguments.html.title: Parameters and Arguments
main/parameters-and-arguments.html.description:
Parameters are Variables defined in the method/function/procedure declaration.
Arguments are the actual values supplied when calling the method/function/procedure.FUNCTION add(a, b) ← a and b are parameters SET result = add(5, 3) ← 5 and 3 are arguments
Method parameters are also called local parameters because they are available within the scope of the method.Parameters can be passed in different ways depending on the programming language or system.A value parameter receives a copy of the value supplied by the caller. The procedure/function can use the value.
Changes made to the parameter generally do not change the caller's original variable.
A reference parameter provides access to the caller's variable or object reference.
Changes made through the parameter can affect the original variable. Useful when a procedure needs to modify a value supplied by the caller. IN JAVA There is no pass-by-reference It still uses pass-by-value but instead we pass the address of the object as the value These parameter modes are commonly used in stored procedures, particularly in SQL/database systems.An IN parameter passes a value into the procedure. Used as input. Can be used in SQL statements and calculations. The procedure does not use it to return a modified value to the caller. CALL procedureName(inputValue) Direction: Caller → ProcedureAn OUT parameter passes a value out of the procedure. Used to return a result from the procedure. The procedure assigns or modifies the parameter. The resulting value can be retrieved by the caller after the procedure executes. Direction: Procedure → Caller An OUT parameter is not necessarily returned as a result set; it is a separate output value. A stored procedure can also return a result set independently. An INOUT parameter combines the behavior of IN and OUT parameters. Receives an initial value from the caller. The procedure can modify that value. The modified value is passed back to the caller. Direction: Caller → Procedure → Caller*The procedure may be able to assign to its local copy depending on the language, but the change is not returned through the parameter.

main/scoping.html.title: Scoping
main/scoping.html.description:
Scope determines where a variable can be accessed or used in a program.
The major variable scopes in Java are:
Variables declared inside a Class but outside any method, constructor, or block. These are usually called fields.
If declared with static, they are Class Variables.
Can be accessed by methods in the Class, depending on their access modifier.
static Variables can be accessed through the Class itself. class Example { static int count = 10; // class variable }
Note: Java does not technically have "global Variables" like some other programming languages. What are often called global Variables are usually Class/static Variables.
Variables declared inside a Class but outside methods, without static.
Each object gets its own copy of the variable.
Also called instance Variables. They can be accessed through an object. class Student { String name; // instance variable int age; // instance variable } Each Student object can have a different name and age.
Variables declared inside a method, constructor, or function-like block. They can only be accessed within the area where they are declared.
They are created when the method/block starts executing and are no longer accessible after it ends. void greet() { String message = "Hello"; // local variable System.out.println(message); } message cannot be accessed outside greet().
Parameters are Variables passed into a method or constructor.
They are only available inside that method or constructor. void greet(String name) { System.out.println("Hello " + name); } Here, name is a parameter and can only be used inside greet(). A block is a section of code enclosed in curly braces {}.
Variables declared inside a block can only be used within that block. Common examples include: if statements for loops while loops switch statements if (true) { int x = 10; System.out.println(x); } // x cannot be accessed here
A variable declared inside the if block is not accessible outside it.
In Java, Variables declared inside a method are local to that method.void first() { int x = 10; } void second() { // x cannot be accessed here }
The variable x belongs only to first().
Java does not have function scope in exactly the same terminology as JavaScript, but method-local Variables have a similar idea: they are accessible only within their method/block.
Hoisting refers to the behavior where variable or function declarations are treated as if they are moved to the top of their scope before execution.
Java does not have JavaScript-style variable hoisting.For example:public class Example { public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println(x); // Error int x = 10; } } This produces an error because x must be declared before it is used.
JavaScript JavaScript has hoisting behavior, but it depends on how the variable is declared: var → declaration is hoisted. let and const → declarations are hoisted internally but cannot be accessed before declaration because of the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ). Function declarations can generally be called before their declaration.

main/serialization.html.title: Serialization
main/serialization.html.description:
Serialization is the process of converting an object in memory into a format that can be stored or transmitted.In Java:Object in memory ↓ Serialization ↓
Sequence of bytes
The resulting bytes can be:
saved to a file
sent over a network
stored for later use
The reverse process is called deserialization:Sequence of bytes ↓ Deserialization ↓
Object in memory
User user = new User("Alice", 20);
Serialization converts the user object into bytes so its state can be stored or transmitted.
Later, deserialization reconstructs the object from those bytes.

main/variables.html.title: Variables
main/variables.html.description:
A variable is a named storage location used to hold a value that can change during program execution. note on initialization: Class variables are implicitly initialized A primitive variable stores a primitive value. Java has eight primitive data types: Example:int age = 20; double price = 19.99; char grade = 'A'; boolean active = true; Conceptually, a primitive variable contains its value directly.age ┌───────┐ │ 20 │ └───────┘ The exact physical memory representation is managed by the JVM and should not be treated as a Java-level memory address.
seealso Casting & Conversion on Assignment
Scoping A reference variable holds a reference to an object rather than the object itself. Example:String name = "Alice"; Conceptually:name │ ▼ ┌─────────────┐ │ "Alice" │ │ Object │ └─────────────┘ A reference is often described as being pointer-like, but Java does not provide direct pointer manipulation like C or C++. You cannot directly access or manipulate an object's memory address in normal Java code.
Classes Interfaces Arrays Enums String
Wrapper classes such as Integer and Double Example:Person person = new Person(); person │ ▼ Person object The variable person contains a reference to the Person object.Garbage Collection To destroy an object (See Garbage Collection) Set the pointer to NULL Set the pointer to a common object to make the original unreachable

Access Modifiers

main/wrapper-classes.html.title: Wrapper Classes
main/wrapper-classes.html.description: All wrapper objects are Immutable Convert primitives into objects Examples: Integer, Double, Boolean, Character, etc. Support autoboxing and auto-unboxing Autoboxing → primitive → wrapper object Auto-unboxing → wrapper object → primitive POJO / Entity Classes Use wrapper types when fields need to be nullable Example: Integer age can be null, while int age cannot Parameter Types Use wrappers when parameters may need to accept null Return Types Use wrappers when a method may return null Computation Avoid wrappers for heavy numerical computation Operations may involve unboxing and boxing, creating unnecessary overhead Sorting Prefer primitive types when sorting large amounts of numerical data Avoid unnecessary boxing/unboxing overhea

info_attractionForce.description: How much should linked nodes attract each other? This will make the graph appear more clustered.

info_linkLength.description: How long should the links between nodes be? The shorter the links the more connected nodes will cluster together.

info_repulsionForce.description: How much should nodes repel each other? This will make disconnected parts more spread out.

info_centralForce.description: How much should nodes be attracted to the center? This will make the graph appear more dense and circular.

info_edgePruning.description: Edges with a length above this threshold will not be rendered, however they will still contribute to the simulation. This can help large tangled graphs look more organised. Hovering over a node will still display these links.

info_minNodeRadius.description: How small should the smallest nodes be? The smaller a node is the less it will attract other nodes.

info_maxNodeRadius.description: How large should the largest nodes be? Nodes are sized by how many links they have. The larger a node is the more it will attract other nodes. This can be used to create a good grouping around the most important nodes.
